blocks.prompt: The Rabbit That Listens
blocks.text: A rabbit is built to listen. Its ears are long and they turn like little cups. One ear can point one way while the other ear points back. Sounds come in from all around. A rabbit is also built to run. Its back legs are long and strong. When a rabbit sees something scary, it stamps its back foot on the ground. Thump. That sound warns every rabbit nearby. Then they all run for the burrow. A burrow is a tunnel a rabbit digs with its front paws. Under the grass there are rooms and doors and long dark halls.

blocks.prompt: Not a Rodent at All
blocks.text: Most people think a rabbit is a rodent, like a mouse or a squirrel. It is not. Scientists put rabbits in a group of their own called lagomorphs. Here is how you can tell. Look behind a rabbit's two big front teeth and you will find two small teeth hiding right behind them. They are called peg teeth. A mouse does not have them. A rabbit does. A rabbit's teeth have another surprise. They never stop growing. They push up a little more every week, for the rabbit's whole life. That sounds like a problem, and it would be, except a rabbit spends hours a day grinding tough grass and hay between them. The chewing wears the teeth down at almost exactly the speed they grow. A rabbit's eyes sit high on the sides of its head. It can see almost all the way around itself without turning. There is one place it cannot see. Straight in front of its own nose. That is why a rabbit will sniff a piece of food it is standing right on top of.

blocks.prompt: The Rabbit Eats Its Dinner Twice
blocks.text: Grass is a terrible meal. It is mostly cellulose, the tough stringy stuff that makes a plant stand up, and almost no animal can break it down alone. A cow solves this with an enormous stomach and hours of standing still. A rabbit is far too small for that, and far too likely to be eaten to stand around anywhere for hours. So the rabbit found a different answer. It eats everything twice. Tucked past a rabbit's stomach is a pouch called the cecum. In a rabbit it is huge, roughly ten times the size of the stomach itself, and it is packed with bacteria. Those bacteria do the work the rabbit cannot. They ferment the cellulose and unlock the nutrition trapped inside it, along with vitamins the rabbit needs. There is one problem. The cecum sits near the end of the line, past most of the gut that absorbs food. All that good nutrition is about to leave the body unused. So the rabbit takes it back. Twice a day, usually in the quiet hours before dawn, the rabbit produces a soft, shiny, grape-like bundle called a cecotrope, and eats it directly, without it ever touching the ground. The cecotrope travels through the whole system a second time, and this time the body absorbs what the bacteria made. A rabbit produces two kinds of droppings: the dry round pellets you find under the hutch, and the cecotropes you almost never see, because they never last long enough to be found. It sounds unpleasant. It is also the only reason a small animal can live on a lawn.

blocks.prompt: Built to Be Hunted
blocks.text: Nearly everything eats rabbits. Foxes, hawks, owls, stoats, snakes, feral cats, eagles. A wild rabbit lives, on average, less than two years, and most of them do not make it past their first few months. Almost every strange thing about a rabbit's body is an answer to that fact. Start with the eyes. They sit high and wide on the sides of the skull, which gives a rabbit a field of view of nearly three hundred and sixty degrees. It can watch the sky behind it while it chews. The cost of that arrangement is a blind spot directly in front of its nose, which is why a rabbit sniffs for food it is standing on. The nose helps. A rabbit twitches it constantly, dragging air across scent cells so it can smell a fox before it ever sees one. Then the ears. They rotate almost independently, so one can track a sound to the left while the other listens right. They do a second job too. A rabbit cannot sweat much, so blood runs close to the surface of those thin ears and sheds heat into the air. The hotter the country, the bigger the ears. Jackrabbits in the American desert have ears so large they look like a mistake, and they are not a mistake at all. Then the escape. Long hind legs, a light skeleton, and a habit of running in hard zigzags rather than straight lines, because a straight line is easy to aim at. A rabbit will thump a back foot on the ground first, a signal that travels through soil to every rabbit in the warren. And then the numbers. A rabbit is pregnant for about thirty-one days, can have up to a dozen young, and can be pregnant again within hours of giving birth. The mother does something that looks cruel. She visits the nest to nurse for roughly five minutes a day, then leaves. Her milk is extremely rich, so five minutes is enough, and staying away means she does not walk a trail of her own scent to her babies. A rabbit is not a fragile animal. It is a solved problem.

notes: Oryctolagus cuniculus, the European rabbit

blocks.prompt: Twenty-Four Rabbits and a Continent
blocks.text: In 1859 a man named Thomas Austin, a landowner in Victoria, Australia, asked his brother in England to send him some rabbits. Austin missed hunting. Twenty-four of them arrived and were released onto his property at Barwon Park around Christmas that year. It was not the first time rabbits had landed in Australia. The First Fleet had carried them in 1788, and settlers had kept them for decades. Those rabbits stayed in their hutches and their small paddocks and did nothing much at all. Austin's did something else. The difference, a genetic study published in 2022 concluded, was in the animals themselves. Earlier arrivals were tame domestic stock, bred for centuries to be calm and slow and dependent. Austin's shipment included rabbits caught wild in the English countryside, and it was their genes that spilled outward. Researchers sampling rabbits from across Australia found the signature of that one small release running through the whole continent. What followed is the fastest invasion by a mammal ever recorded. The rabbits pushed outward at roughly one hundred kilometers a year. Australia had handed them a country with mild winters, endless grass, soft soil for digging, and almost no predator that had ever learned to hunt them. Within seventy years the population was estimated in the billions. They stripped seedlings before the seedlings could become trees. They cut grazing land out from under sheep. They dug until hillsides lost their topsoil to the wind. Native animals that ate the same plants, the bilby and the bettong among them, were pushed toward extinction, and some went over the edge. Australia fought back, and the scale of the fighting is difficult to imagine now. Between 1901 and 1907, Western Australia built a fence. Fence No. 1 ran for more than eighteen hundred kilometers, from the north coast to the south, the longest unbroken fence in the world. It was a serious, expensive, well-built structure, and it did not work. By the time the last post went in, rabbits were already breeding on the far side of it. The fence had been outrun during its own construction. In 1950 the government tried biology instead, releasing myxomatosis, a virus deadly to European rabbits. It worked spectacularly and briefly. Something close to ninety-nine percent of the rabbits died. Then the survivors bred, and their descendants carried resistance. The virus also grew milder, because a virus that kills its host too quickly has nowhere left to go. Within a decade the kill rate had collapsed. A second virus arrived in 1995 and repeated the pattern: a huge crash, then a slow recovery. Rabbits are still there. They still cost Australian agriculture hundreds of millions of dollars a year, and the control programs run without an end date. It is tempting to file this under things rabbits did. That is not quite honest. The rabbit did nothing it was not built to do. It ate, it dug, it bred at the rate a hunted animal breeds when nothing is hunting it. Twenty-four animals stepped off a ship into a place with no answer for them, and the animals behaved exactly as animals behave. The decision was made by someone who wanted a familiar afternoon's sport, and the continent has been paying for that afternoon for more than a century and a half.
